abstract: >
  **Importance:** Several professional medical societies have removed race and ethnicity from widely used clinical algorithms with implications for millions. Yet, patient and public opinions regarding the tensions underlying these pivotal changes have not been systematically explored.\

  **Objective:**  To assess global public opinion on the use of race or ethnicity in clinical algorithms, including preferences for different approaches to algorithmic reform and perceptions of alternative predictors.\

  **Design:** Cross-sectional survey study.\

  **Setting:** Multinational opt-in online survey in January 2026.\

  **Participants:** A volunteer convenience sample with quota sampling to achieve approximately equal participation by sex at birth and across ten categories of self-identified race and ethnicity.\

  **Main Outcomes and Measures:** Self-reported comfort with demographic and social predictors in clinical calculators, with net comfort defined as percentage extremely or somewhat comfortable minus percentage extremely or somewhat uncomfortable; preferences for race-specific versus race-free algorithms; perceptions of algorithmic harm or benefit.\

  **Results:** Of 1,050 responses, 994 (94.7%) met eligibility criteria. Participants resided in 43 countries with a median age of 32.0 years (IQR, 26-41). Net comfort with the use of race or ethnicity in a hypothetical cancer risk calculator was +62.4% (95% CI: +57.8% to +66.9%), compared with +14.5% (95% CI: +9.1% to +19.9%) for postal or ZIP code. Overall, 87.9% (95% CI: 85.9% to 90.0%) were comfortable with the use of race or ethnicity if a clinician explained its use, and only 12.8% agreed race and ethnicity should never be used clinically. Across spirometry, kidney function, and cardiovascular risk calculators, 40.0% to 47.6% preferred race-specific versions, whereas 16.7% to 28.2% preferred race-free alternatives. Furthermore, a substantial proportion disagreed that they were well-represented by race and ethnicity categories, ranging from 22.1% for osteoporotic fracture risk equations to 42.9% for cardiovascular risk equations. These findings were consistent across countries, self-identified race and ethnicity, and among participants reporting prior experiences of racism in healthcare.\
  
  **Conclusions and Relevance:** In our diverse multinational survey study, respondents were comfortable with the use of race and ethnicity across application areas, but often did not feel represented by existing categories and were less comfortable with alternatives based on postal or ZIP codes.

bibliography: references.bib
csl: jama.csl

# Simplify reaction labels based on actual response text
simplify_reaction <- function(x) {
  case_when(
    # Race-based preferences (various phrasings across algorithms)
    str_detect(x, "takes my race or ethnicity into account") ~ "Prefer race-based",
    str_detect(x, "race or ethnicity is considered") ~ "Prefer race-based",
    # Race-free preferences
    str_detect(x, "does not depend on race") ~ "Prefer race-free",
    str_detect(x, "does not consider my race") ~ "Prefer race-free",
    str_detect(x, "postal or zip code instead") ~ "Prefer postal-ZIP instead of race",
    # Neutral
    str_detect(x, regex("neutral|unsure", ignore_case = TRUE)) ~ "Neutral/Unsure",
    # Other
    str_detect(x, "self-describe") ~ "Other",
    TRUE ~ NA_character_
  )
}

## Introduction

Since 2019, there has been a movement to reconsider the use of race and ethnicity in clinical equations and algorithms [@Vyas2020; @Nkinsi2022]. As of April 2026, several professional societies have removed race as an explicit input from clinical algorithms used to estimate spirometry reference standards [@bhakta2023; @Bowerman2023], kidney function [@Delgado2022], cardiovascular risk for treating dyslipidemia and hypertension [@khan2024; @jones_2025; @Morris_2026], and risk of vaginal birth after caesarean [@the_american_college_of_obstetricians_and_gynecologists_practice_2021]. Other medical societies, including the International Osteoporosis Foundation and the Society of Thoracic Surgeons have resisted calls to remove race from their risk calculators, citing unacceptable accuracy loss [@macgillivray_impact_2023; @shahian_social_2022] particularly for minority groups in the US [@kanis_race-specific_2024].

A critical gap in the debate over race or ethnicity in clinical algorithms has been the relative absence of global patient and public perspectives [@bhakta2023]. Patient and public opinion studies on this topic have focused on the US [@schmidt2023; @jain2023; @diao2026], even though some of these algorithms are deployed globally [@braun_breathing_2014]. The broader debate has also been largely US-centric [@chellappoo_race_2024; @doh_position_2025; @jaime_ethnic_2024].

Here, we report a multinational survey on race or ethnicity and algorithmic reform in medicine, focusing on four guideline-referenced algorithms representing different reform approaches (@tbl-algorithms). Our sample was non-representative but diverse, recruited from opt-in online participants living in 43 countries across six continents, with quota-sampling to ensure equal participation by sex and ten self-identified categories of race and ethnicity.

::: {#tbl-algorithms style="font-size: 0.75em;"}
| Original Algorithm | Purpose | Race/Ethnicity Categories | Revised Algorithm | Reform | Professional Society | Ref. |
|:----------|:----------|:----------|:----------|:----------|:----------|-----------|
| 2009 CKD-EPI | Glomerular Filtration Rate (GFR) | Black, Non-Black | 2021 CKD-EPI | Refit without race | National Kidney Foundation, American Society of Nephrology | [@Delgado2022] |
| GLI-2012 | Spirometry Reference Values | White, African American, Northeast Asian, Southeast Asian, Other | GLI-Global 2022 | Race-averaged | American Thoracic Society, European Respiratory Society | [@bhakta2023; @Bowerman2023] |
| Pooled Cohort Equations | 10-year risk for total cardiovascular disease | White, African American, Other^1^ | PREVENT | Replaced race with optional ZIP code | American Heart Association | [@khan2024; @jones_2025; @Morris_2026] |
| FRAX | 10-year risk of bone fracture | Brunei: Chinese; Malaysia: Bumiputera, Chinese, Indian; Singapore: Chinese, Indian, Malay; South Africa: African, Coloured, Indian, White; USA: Asian, Black, White, Hispanic; All other countries: single model, not ethnicity-specific^2^ | -- | -- | International Osteoporosis Foundation | [@kanis_race-specific_2024] |

: Overview of Clinical Algorithms Included in the Survey
:::

^1^ The "other" category exists in pooled cohort web calculator but not in the underlying statistical model. In the web app, it uses the "White" value alongside a warning that the results might under- or overestimate risk for certain population groups.

^2^ Ethnicity sub-categories are shown per FRAX v1.4.8.


## Methods

### Questionnaire Design

The questionnaire was iteratively drafted with feedback from six graduate students (epidemiology, health outcomes, clinical prediction modelling) and three faculty members (medicine, clinical prediction, algorithmic fairness), then revised further after pretesting via cognitive interviews with two patient partners. The exact wording of the questionnaire is in the appendix.

After a plain-language explainer about clinical calculators, the questionnaire presented four calculators reflecting different reform approaches in randomized order: refitting without race (eGFR), race‑averaged reference values (spirometry), replacing race with an area‑based deprivation score from postal codes (PREVENT), and retaining race or ethnicity (FRAX). For each, we asked whether participants felt represented by its categories, whether using race or ethnicity could improve their care, and whether they worried it might cause harm, using Likert‑scale items with randomized response direction. After all four sections, participants saw the race-free version (where available) and chose which they preferred.

Comfort with different predictors was assessed via a hypothetical cancer risk calculator, with five-point ratings for: home postal or ZIP code, race or ethnicity, genetic ancestry, biological sex, country of origin, age, and environmental exposures.

Participants were asked if they had ever felt being treated unfairly in the healthcare system because of their race or ethnicity, with an optional open-ended follow-up to describe their experience. A second item asked whether clinic staff had ever recorded their race or ethnicity without asking.

Four replication items enabled comparison with prior representative US surveys, covering whether doctors should use race or ethnicity in clinical care, perceptions of bias in health and medicine, and expectations of care from racially or ethnically concordant providers [@diao2026].

### Survey Recruitment

We recruited participants through Prolific, with quota sampling for equal participation by biological sex at birth and ten self-identified ethnicity groups previously collected by Prolific. The survey was distributed over four waves at midnight and noon Pacific Time in January 2026. To expand geographical diversity, residents of countries exceeding 100 responses were excluded from subsequent waves. Participants consented at the beginning and end of the survey. Those who completed the study and passed authenticity checks were reimbursed at an average rate of £9.72/hour.

### Demographics

Self-identified data on age, sex, gender, ethnicity, countries of residence and birth, employment, and socioeconomic status were collected by Prolific prior to the survey. Prolific's ethnicity field required a single category; an additional survey item asked participants to select all population groups that applied (or self-describe), with options including African, African American, Caribbean, East Asian, Hispanic or Latina/Latino, Indigenous, Middle Eastern and North African, South Asian, Southeast Asian, and White (full wording in the appendix).

### Analysis
The study adhered to the AAPOR best practices. Open-ended responses were analyzed by conventional content analysis [@hsieh2005] in NVivo v1.7.2; non-English responses were translated via Google Translate and cross-checked with DeepL. Two reviewers independently developed a shared codebook through open coding of a subset of responses, then independently applied it to 10% of responses per question to ensure consistency. After discrepancies were resolved by consensus, the remaining responses were coded by one reviewer. Codes were grouped into broader categories by conceptual similarity, frequencies tallied, and representative quotes selected. Quantitative analyses were descriptive and unweighted, performed in Quarto v1.9.30 and R v4.5.2 with 95% confidence intervals from 2000 nonparametric bootstrap resamples.

### Ethics Approval

The study was approved by the Behavioural Research Ethics Board at the University of British Columbia (H25-02789).

## Results

Of 1,050 responses received, 48 participants revoked consent, 6 timed out, and 2 failed authenticity checks. The remaining 994 participants lived in 43 countries (@suppfig-top-country-residence), were born in 87 (@suppfig-top-country-birth), and had a median age of 32.0 years (IQR, 26-41). Among them, 500 (50.3%) were female and 494 (49.7%) were male by sex as recorded on legal/official documents. For the subset with gender identity data available, 50.1% identified as women, 48.4% as men, and 1.6% as non-binary. Overall, 53.1% worked full-time and 23.7% had a background in healthcare or health sciences (@tbl-1; characteristics stratified by ethnicity in @supptab-characteristics-by-ethnicity). Quantitative survey responses were largely complete, with no variable missing for more than 0.7% of participants.

### Perceptions of Race and Ethnicity

Participants were asked to describe what "race or ethnicity" meant to them. Of 993 substantive responses analyzed, three (Portuguese, Polish, Spanish) were translated before non-mutually exclusive coding. Many defined race and ethnicity in terms of physical traits and skin colour (37.3%), place of origin (26.8%), ancestry (22.8%), and genetics (17.0%), while fewer described them as social constructs (2.9%). About 12.4% explicitly defined race and ethnicity as distinct concepts—the former relating to visible physical characteristics and the latter relating to cultural background or upbringing. Some (7.0%) described race and ethnicity as central to their identity, providing togetherness, belonging, and pride. A small subset (4.5%) noted perceived differences in disease risk across racial or ethnic groups. The codebook (@supptab-codebook-race), code frequencies (@supptab-codebook-freq), and example responses are in the Appendix.

### Comfort Level for Different Predictors

```{r}
#| label: calc-net-comfort-stats
#| output: false

comfort_pos <- c("Somewhat comfortable", "Extremely comfortable")
comfort_neg <- c("Somewhat uncomfortable", "Extremely uncomfortable")

net_comfort <- function(x) {
  x <- x[!is.na(x)]
  (mean(x %in% comfort_pos) - mean(x %in% comfort_neg)) * 100
}

boot_ci_net <- function(x, R = 2000) {
  x <- x[!is.na(x)]
  reps <- replicate(R, {
    s <- sample(x, length(x), replace = TRUE)
    (mean(s %in% comfort_pos) - mean(s %in% comfort_neg)) * 100
  })
  quantile(reps, c(0.025, 0.975), names = FALSE)
}

fmt_ci_signed       <- function(p, ci) sprintf("%+.1f%% (95%% CI: %+.1f to %+.1f)", p, ci[1], ci[2])
fmt_ci_signed_inner <- function(p, ci) sprintf("%+.1f%%, 95%% CI: %+.1f to %+.1f",   p, ci[1], ci[2])

# Per-factor net comfort + 95% CI
nc_age      <- net_comfort(responses[["fd-factors_1"]]); ci_nc_age      <- boot_ci_net(responses[["fd-factors_1"]])
nc_sex      <- net_comfort(responses[["fd-factors_2"]]); ci_nc_sex      <- boot_ci_net(responses[["fd-factors_2"]])
nc_race     <- net_comfort(responses[["fd-factors_3"]]); ci_nc_race     <- boot_ci_net(responses[["fd-factors_3"]])
nc_zip      <- net_comfort(responses[["fd-factors_4"]]); ci_nc_zip      <- boot_ci_net(responses[["fd-factors_4"]])
nc_env      <- net_comfort(responses[["fd-factors_5"]]); ci_nc_env      <- boot_ci_net(responses[["fd-factors_5"]])
nc_ancestry <- net_comfort(responses[["fd-factors_6"]]); ci_nc_ancestry <- boot_ci_net(responses[["fd-factors_6"]])
nc_country  <- net_comfort(responses[["fd-factors_7"]]); ci_nc_country  <- boot_ci_net(responses[["fd-factors_7"]])

pct_comfort <- function(x) {
  x <- x[!is.na(x)]
  mean(x %in% comfort_pos) * 100
}
boot_ci_pct_comfort <- function(x, R = 2000) {
  x <- x[!is.na(x)]
  reps <- replicate(R, mean(sample(x, length(x), replace = TRUE) %in% comfort_pos) * 100)
  quantile(reps, c(0.025, 0.975), names = FALSE)
}
pct_race_comfort <- pct_comfort(responses[["fd-factors_3"]])
ci_pct_race_comfort <- boot_ci_pct_comfort(responses[["fd-factors_3"]])

# Per-ethnicity net comfort (multi-select expansion)
eth_patterns <- c(
  "African"          = "African \\(",
  "East Asian"       = "East Asian",
  "Hispanic/Latino"  = "Hispanic",
  "South Asian"      = "(?<!east )South Asian"
)

eth_long <- responses |>
  filter(!is.na(`demo-ethnicity`)) |>
  rowwise() |>
  mutate(eth_list = list(names(eth_patterns)[
    sapply(eth_patterns, \(pat) str_detect(`demo-ethnicity`, pat))
  ])) |>
  ungroup() |>
  unnest(eth_list)

nc_eth <- function(eth, var) {
  v <- eth_long[[var]][eth_long$eth_list == eth]
  list(pct = net_comfort(v), ci = boot_ci_net(v))
}

nc_race_african    <- nc_eth("African",         "fd-factors_3")
nc_race_eastasian  <- nc_eth("East Asian",      "fd-factors_3")
nc_zip_hispanic    <- nc_eth("Hispanic/Latino", "fd-factors_4")
nc_zip_southasian  <- nc_eth("South Asian",     "fd-factors_4")
```

Respondents rated their comfort with a hypothetical cancer risk calculator using various inputs. We define net comfort as the percentage extremely or somewhat comfortable minus the percentage extremely or somewhat uncomfortable. Most were comfortable with age (net comfort `r fmt_ci_signed_inner(nc_age, ci_nc_age)`), biological sex (`r fmt_ci_signed_inner(nc_sex, ci_nc_sex)`), environmental exposures (`r fmt_ci_signed_inner(nc_env, ci_nc_env)`), and genetic ancestry (`r fmt_ci_signed_inner(nc_ancestry, ci_nc_ancestry)`). Comfort declined for country of origin (`r fmt_ci_signed_inner(nc_country, ci_nc_country)`) and race and ethnicity (`r fmt_ci_signed_inner(nc_race, ci_nc_race)`), and much lower for ZIP or postal code (`r fmt_ci_signed_inner(nc_zip, ci_nc_zip)`; @fig-comfort-factor).

Comfort varied across participants (@suppfig-ethnicity-self-comfort-factor, @suppfig-ethnicity-comfort-factor): net comfort with race and ethnicity ranged from `r fmt_ci_signed(nc_race_african$pct, nc_race_african$ci)` among Africans to `r fmt_ci_signed(nc_race_eastasian$pct, nc_race_eastasian$ci)` among East Asians, and for ZIP or postal code from `r fmt_ci_signed(nc_zip_hispanic$pct, nc_zip_hispanic$ci)` among Hispanic/Latino to `r fmt_ci_signed(nc_zip_southasian$pct, nc_zip_southasian$ci)` among South Asians. Among countries with ≥20 respondents, net comfort remained positive for race and ethnicity, but was sometimes negative for ZIP or postal code (@suppfig-country-comfort-factor).

```{r}
#| label: calc-never-use-stats
#| output: false

# rep-diao_1: comfortable if doctor believes it is best for care
# rep-diao_2: comfortable if doctor discusses how and why it is used
# rep-diao_3: comfortable if recommended by practice guidelines
# rep-diao_4: doctors should never use race or ethnicity (agree = oppose use)

calc_pct_agree <- function(col) {
  x <- responses[[col]]
  x <- x[!is.na(x)]
  sum(x %in% c("Somewhat agree", "Strongly agree")) / length(x) * 100
}

# Percentile bootstrap 95% CI for a proportion (returned as %)
boot_ci_agree <- function(x, R = 2000) {
  x <- x[!is.na(x)]
  reps <- replicate(R, {
    s <- sample(x, length(x), replace = TRUE)
    mean(s %in% c("Somewhat agree", "Strongly agree")) * 100
  })
  quantile(reps, c(0.025, 0.975), names = FALSE)
}

ci_discussed  <- boot_ci_agree(responses[["rep-diao_2"]])
ci_guidelines <- boot_ci_agree(responses[["rep-diao_3"]])
ci_best_care  <- boot_ci_agree(responses[["rep-diao_1"]])
ci_never_use  <- boot_ci_agree(responses[["rep-diao_4"]])

pct_discussed    <- calc_pct_agree("rep-diao_2")  # 88%
pct_guidelines   <- calc_pct_agree("rep-diao_3")  # 80%
pct_best_care    <- calc_pct_agree("rep-diao_1")  # 79%
pct_never_use    <- calc_pct_agree("rep-diao_4")  # 13%

fmt_ci <- function(p, ci) sprintf("%.1f%% (95%% CI: %.1f–%.1f)", p, ci[1], ci[2])
fmt_ci_inner <- function(p, ci) sprintf("%.1f%%, 95%% CI: %.1f–%.1f", p, ci[1], ci[2])

# ethnicity_categories is defined later in the document; redefined here for early use
ethnicity_categories_early <- c(
  "African" = "African \\(",
  "African American" = "African American",
  "Caribbean" = "Caribbean",
  "East Asian" = "East Asian",
  "Hispanic/Latino" = "Hispanic",
  "Indigenous" = "Indigenous",
  "Middle Eastern" = "Middle Eastern",
  "Mixed" = "Mixed",
  "South Asian" = "South Asian",
  "Southeast Asian" = "Southeast Asian",
  "White" = "White"
)

# Never-use by self-reported ethnicity (with bootstrap 95% CI per group)
never_use_long <- responses |>
  filter(!is.na(`demo-ethnicity`), !is.na(`rep-diao_4`)) |>
  rowwise() |>
  mutate(eth_list = list(names(ethnicity_categories_early)[
    sapply(ethnicity_categories_early, \(pat) str_detect(`demo-ethnicity`, pat))
  ])) |>
  ungroup() |>
  unnest(eth_list)

never_use_by_self_eth <- never_use_long |>
  group_by(eth_list) |>
  summarise(pct_agree = mean(`rep-diao_4` %in% c("Somewhat agree", "Strongly agree")) * 100,
            .groups = "drop")

ci_never_white <- boot_ci_agree(
  never_use_long$`rep-diao_4`[never_use_long$eth_list == "White"]
)
ci_never_aa <- boot_ci_agree(
  never_use_long$`rep-diao_4`[never_use_long$eth_list == "African American"]
)

pct_never_white <- never_use_by_self_eth$pct_agree[never_use_by_self_eth$eth_list == "White"]
pct_never_aa    <- never_use_by_self_eth$pct_agree[never_use_by_self_eth$eth_list == "African American"]
```

Overall, `r fmt_ci(pct_discussed, ci_discussed)` were comfortable with race or ethnicity in clinical algorithms if the doctor explained why and how it was used, `r fmt_ci(pct_guidelines, ci_guidelines)` if recommended by guidelines, and `r fmt_ci(pct_best_care, ci_best_care)` if the doctor believed it best for care. Only `r fmt_ci(pct_never_use, ci_never_use)` agreed that doctors should never use race or ethnicity, ranging from `r fmt_ci(pct_never_white, ci_never_white)` among White respondents to `r fmt_ci(pct_never_aa, ci_never_aa)` among African Americans (@suppfig-never-use-by-ethnicity).

```{r}
#| label: calc-told-howoften-stats
#| output: false

# Percentile bootstrap 95% CI for proportion of x matching `targets` (returned as %)
boot_ci_match <- function(x, targets, R = 2000) {
  x <- x[!is.na(x)]
  reps <- replicate(R, {
    s <- sample(x, length(x), replace = TRUE)
    mean(s %in% targets) * 100
  })
  quantile(reps, c(0.025, 0.975), names = FALSE)
}

pct_match <- function(x, targets) {
  x <- x[!is.na(x)]
  mean(x %in% targets) * 100
}

told_x   <- responses[["told-race-used"]]
pct_told <- pct_match(told_x, "Yes")
ci_told  <- boot_ci_match(told_x, "Yes")

how_x <- responses[["rep-how-often"]]
pct_always    <- pct_match(how_x, "Always")
pct_most      <- pct_match(how_x, "Most of the time")
pct_half      <- pct_match(how_x, "About half the time")
pct_sometimes <- pct_match(how_x, "Sometimes")
pct_never_ho  <- pct_match(how_x, "Never")

ci_always    <- boot_ci_match(how_x, "Always")
ci_most      <- boot_ci_match(how_x, "Most of the time")
ci_half      <- boot_ci_match(how_x, "About half the time")
ci_sometimes <- boot_ci_match(how_x, "Sometimes")
ci_never_ho  <- boot_ci_match(how_x, "Never")
```

About `r fmt_ci(pct_told, ci_told)` recalled a clinician telling them their race or ethnicity played a role in a medical decision. When asked how often they are asked for race or ethnicity in healthcare settings, `r fmt_ci(pct_always, ci_always)` said always, `r fmt_ci(pct_most, ci_most)` most of the time, `r fmt_ci(pct_half, ci_half)` about half, `r fmt_ci(pct_sometimes, ci_sometimes)` sometimes, and `r fmt_ci(pct_never_ho, ci_never_ho)` never. Participants from the UK, US, and South Africa, and those self-identifying as Indigenous, African, Caribbean, or African American were more likely to report being routinely asked (@suppfig-how-often-by-country, @suppfig-how-often-by-ethnicity).

```{r}
#| label: fig-comfort-factor
#| fig-width: 9
#| fig-height: 5
#| fig-cap: "Respondent comfort levels with the use of each demographic and clinical factor in a hypothetical cancer risk calculator. Participants were asked: \"Imagine a doctor is using a clinical calculator to determine your risk for a type of cancer. How comfortable are you with the calculator using each of the following pieces of information?\" Bars extend rightward for comfortable responses (light and dark blue) and leftward for uncomfortable responses (light and dark red), with neutral responses (grey) centred at zero. Factors are ordered by net comfort (total percentage extremely or somewhat comfortable minus total percentage extremely or somewhat uncomfortable)."

factor_vars <- c("fd-factors_1", "fd-factors_2", "fd-factors_3",
                 "fd-factors_4", "fd-factors_5", "fd-factors_6", "fd-factors_7")
factor_labels <- c("Age", "Biological sex", "Race/ethnicity",
                   "ZIP or Postal Code", "Environmental exposures", "Genetic ancestry", "Country of origin")

comfort_levels <- c("Extremely uncomfortable", "Somewhat uncomfortable",
                     "Neither comfortable nor uncomfortable",
                     "Somewhat comfortable", "Extremely comfortable")

comfort_df <- responses |>
  select(all_of(factor_vars)) |>
  setNames(factor_labels) |>
  pivot_longer(everything(), names_to = "factor", values_to = "comfort") |>
  filter(!is.na(comfort)) |>
  mutate(comfort = factor(comfort, levels = comfort_levels))

# Percentages per factor-level combination
comfort_summary <- comfort_df |>
  count(factor, comfort) |>
  group_by(factor) |>
  mutate(pct = n / sum(n) * 100) |>
  ungroup()

# Order factors by net comfort
factor_order <- comfort_summary |>
  mutate(side = case_when(
    comfort %in% c("Somewhat comfortable", "Extremely comfortable") ~ "pos",
    comfort %in% c("Somewhat uncomfortable", "Extremely uncomfortable") ~ "neg",
    TRUE ~ "neutral"
  )) |>
  group_by(factor) |>
  summarise(
    net = sum(pct[side == "pos"]) - sum(pct[side == "neg"]),
    .groups = "drop"
  ) |>
  arrange(net) |>
  pull(factor)

# Build diverging positions: uncomfortable goes left, neutral centred, comfortable goes right
comfort_plot <- comfort_summary |>
  mutate(factor = factor(factor, levels = factor_order)) |>
  group_by(factor) |>
  mutate(
    # Half of neutral straddles zero
    neutral_pct = pct[comfort == "Neither comfortable nor uncomfortable"],
    # Cumulative negative side (extremely uncomf, then somewhat uncomf, then half neutral)
    xmin = case_when(
      comfort == "Extremely uncomfortable" ~
        -(pct[comfort == "Extremely uncomfortable"] +
          pct[comfort == "Somewhat uncomfortable"] +
          neutral_pct / 2),
      comfort == "Somewhat uncomfortable" ~
        -(pct[comfort == "Somewhat uncomfortable"] +
          neutral_pct / 2),
      comfort == "Neither comfortable nor uncomfortable" ~
        -(neutral_pct / 2),
      comfort == "Somewhat comfortable" ~
        neutral_pct / 2,
      comfort == "Extremely comfortable" ~
        neutral_pct / 2 + pct[comfort == "Somewhat comfortable"]
    ),
    xmax = xmin + pct
  ) |>
  ungroup()

# Net comfort labels
net_labels <- comfort_plot |>
  group_by(factor) |>
  summarise(
    net = sum(pct[comfort %in% c("Somewhat comfortable", "Extremely comfortable")]) -
          sum(pct[comfort %in% c("Somewhat uncomfortable", "Extremely uncomfortable")]),
    x_end = max(xmax),
    .groups = "drop"
  )

ggplot(comfort_plot, aes(y = factor, xmin = xmin, xmax = xmax, fill = comfort)) +
  geom_rect(aes(ymin = as.numeric(factor) - 0.35,
                ymax = as.numeric(factor) + 0.35)) +
  geom_text(aes(x = (xmin + xmax) / 2, y = factor,
                label = ifelse(abs(xmax - xmin) > 6, sprintf("%.1f%%", pct), "")),
            size = 3) +
  geom_text(data = net_labels,
            aes(x = x_end + 2, y = factor, label = sprintf("%+.1f%%", net)),
            inherit.aes = FALSE, size = 3.5, hjust = 0) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = 0, linewidth = 0.3, alpha = 0.3) +
  scale_fill_manual(
    values = c(
      "Extremely uncomfortable" = "#d73027",
      "Somewhat uncomfortable"  = "#fc8d59",
      "Neither comfortable nor uncomfortable" = "#cccccc",
      "Somewhat comfortable"    = "#91bfdb",
      "Extremely comfortable"   = "#4575b4"
    ),
    name = NULL,
    breaks = comfort_levels
  ) +
  scale_x_continuous(labels = \(x) paste0(abs(x), "%"),
                     expand = expansion(mult = c(0.05, 0.12))) +
  labs(x = NULL, y = NULL) +
  theme_minimal() +
  guides(fill = guide_legend(nrow = 2, byrow = TRUE)) +
  theme(legend.position = "top",
        legend.text = element_text(size = 8))
```

### Algorithmic Reform

```{r}
#| label: race_how_often
#| output: false

# question: When you are seeking healthcare, how often are you asked what race or ethnicity group you belong to (either by the doctor or on a form)?
responses |>
   filter(!is.na(`rep-how-often`)) |>
   count(`rep-how-often`) |>
   mutate(pct = round(n / sum(n) * 100, 2))

# question: Have you ever had the experience of noticing that a doctor, nurse, or clinic staff have filled out your race or ethnicity on a form or computer screen without asking you?
responses |>
   filter(!is.na(`rep-misclassify`)) |>
   count(`rep-misclassify`) |>
   mutate(pct = round(n / sum(n) * 100, 2))

```

```{r}
#| label: calc-misclassify-stats
#| output: false

mis_x <- responses[["rep-misclassify"]]
yes_any <- c("Yes, and it did not match my own choice",
             "Yes, and it matched my own choice")
mismatch <- "Yes, and it did not match my own choice"

pct_filled_without_asking <- pct_match(mis_x, yes_any)
ci_filled_without_asking  <- boot_ci_match(mis_x, yes_any)

pct_misidentified <- pct_match(mis_x, mismatch)
ci_misidentified  <- boot_ci_match(mis_x, mismatch)
```

About `r fmt_ci(pct_filled_without_asking, ci_filled_without_asking)` reported staff filling out their race or ethnicity without asking them to self-identify; about a quarter of those (`r fmt_ci(pct_misidentified, ci_misidentified)` of total) experienced misidentification. This was most common in Kenya and South Africa (@suppfig-misclassify-by-country) and among Indigenous, African, African American, and Caribbean participants (@suppfig-misclassify-by-ethnicity).

```{r}
#| label: calc-represented-net-stats
#| output: false

likert_pos <- c("Somewhat agree", "Strongly agree")
likert_neg <- c("Somewhat disagree", "Strongly disagree")

net_agree <- function(x) {
  x <- x[!is.na(x)]
  (mean(x %in% likert_pos) - mean(x %in% likert_neg)) * 100
}

boot_ci_net_agree <- function(x, R = 2000) {
  x <- x[!is.na(x)]
  reps <- replicate(R, {
    s <- sample(x, length(x), replace = TRUE)
    (mean(s %in% likert_pos) - mean(s %in% likert_neg)) * 100
  })
  quantile(reps, c(0.025, 0.975), names = FALSE)
}

na_rep_pooled <- net_agree(responses[["cvd-questions_1"]])
ci_rep_pooled <- boot_ci_net_agree(responses[["cvd-questions_1"]])
na_rep_frax   <- net_agree(responses[["frax-questions_1"]])
ci_rep_frax   <- boot_ci_net_agree(responses[["frax-questions_1"]])

pct_agree_likert <- function(x) {
  x <- x[!is.na(x)]
  mean(x %in% likert_pos) * 100
}
helps_pcts <- sapply(
  c("spiro-questions_3", "egfr-questions_3", "cvd-questions_3", "frax-questions_3"),
  \(v) pct_agree_likert(responses[[v]])
)
helps_lo <- min(helps_pcts)
helps_hi <- max(helps_pcts)
```

Across all four race-specific tools (@fig-reaction), a majority felt represented by the provided racial categories (44.8--64.8% agreement, net agreement from `r fmt_ci_signed_inner(na_rep_pooled, ci_rep_pooled)` for Pooled Cohort which had binary race categories to `r fmt_ci_signed_inner(na_rep_frax, ci_rep_frax)` for FRAX, which is country-specific and ethnicity-specific in certain countries) and believed incorporating race helped improve their care (55.5--58.0%, net +33.9% to +40.1%). Roughly half disagreed that using race or ethnicity could cause harm (net -21.2% to -28.5%).

```{r}
#| label: calc-revised-reaction-stats
#| output: false

spiro_react <- simplify_reaction(responses[["spiro-new-reaction"]])
egfr_react  <- simplify_reaction(responses[["egfr-new-reaction"]])
cvd_react   <- simplify_reaction(responses[["cvd-new-reaction"]])

pct_spiro_rb  <- pct_match(spiro_react, "Prefer race-based")
ci_spiro_rb   <- boot_ci_match(spiro_react, "Prefer race-based")
pct_spiro_rf  <- pct_match(spiro_react, "Prefer race-free")
ci_spiro_rf   <- boot_ci_match(spiro_react, "Prefer race-free")

pct_egfr_rb   <- pct_match(egfr_react, "Prefer race-based")
ci_egfr_rb    <- boot_ci_match(egfr_react, "Prefer race-based")
pct_egfr_rf   <- pct_match(egfr_react, "Prefer race-free")
ci_egfr_rf    <- boot_ci_match(egfr_react, "Prefer race-free")

pct_cvd_rb    <- pct_match(cvd_react, "Prefer race-based")
ci_cvd_rb     <- boot_ci_match(cvd_react, "Prefer race-based")
pct_cvd_zip   <- pct_match(cvd_react, "Prefer postal-ZIP instead of race")
ci_cvd_zip    <- boot_ci_match(cvd_react, "Prefer postal-ZIP instead of race")

# Neutral/Unsure across the three algorithm pairs
pct_neutral_vec <- c(
  pct_match(spiro_react, "Neutral/Unsure"),
  pct_match(egfr_react,  "Neutral/Unsure"),
  pct_match(cvd_react,   "Neutral/Unsure")
)
neutral_lo <- min(pct_neutral_vec)
neutral_hi <- max(pct_neutral_vec)

# Race-based vs race-free (or postal-ZIP for PREVENT) preference ratios
rb_alt_ratios <- c(
  pct_spiro_rb / pct_spiro_rf,
  pct_egfr_rb  / pct_egfr_rf,
  pct_cvd_rb   / pct_cvd_zip
)
rb_ratio_lo <- min(rb_alt_ratios)
rb_ratio_hi <- max(rb_alt_ratios)
```

Respondents did not uniformly embrace revised algorithms that no longer used race and ethnicity: `r fmt_ci(pct_spiro_rb, ci_spiro_rb)` and `r fmt_ci(pct_egfr_rb, ci_egfr_rb)` preferred the race-based versions of spirometry (GLI-2012) and eGFR (2009 CKD-EPI), versus `r fmt_ci(pct_spiro_rf, ci_spiro_rf)` and `r fmt_ci(pct_egfr_rf, ci_egfr_rf)` who favoured the revised replacements (@fig-reaction). For cardiovascular risk, `r fmt_ci(pct_cvd_rb, ci_cvd_rb)` preferred the race-based Pooled Cohort over `r fmt_ci(pct_cvd_zip, ci_cvd_zip)` who preferred PREVENT, which replaces race with optional ZIP code as a socioeconomic proxy. `r sprintf("%.1f--%.1f%%", neutral_lo, neutral_hi)` remained neutral or unsure across all three pairs.

```{r}
#| label: ai_concern
#| output: false

# question: Clinical algorithms can range from simple formulas to complex AI systems. Would your concerns about using race or ethnicity differ depending on the type of tool?
responses |>
   filter(!is.na(`fd-ai-concern`)) |>
   count(`fd-ai-concern`) |>
   mutate(pct = n / sum(n) * 100)

```

```{r}
#| label: calc-ai-concern-stats
#| output: false

ai_x <- responses[["fd-ai-concern"]]
ai_none   <- "I'm not concerned about race or ethnicity being used in any tools."
ai_equal  <- "I would be equally concerned regardless the type of tool."
ai_more   <- "I would be more concerned about race or ethnicity in AI systems than in simple formulas."
ai_less   <- "I would be less concerned about race or ethnicity in AI systems than in simple formulas."

pct_ai_none  <- pct_match(ai_x, ai_none);  ci_ai_none  <- boot_ci_match(ai_x, ai_none)
pct_ai_equal <- pct_match(ai_x, ai_equal); ci_ai_equal <- boot_ci_match(ai_x, ai_equal)
pct_ai_more  <- pct_match(ai_x, ai_more);  ci_ai_more  <- boot_ci_match(ai_x, ai_more)
pct_ai_less  <- pct_match(ai_x, ai_less);  ci_ai_less  <- boot_ci_match(ai_x, ai_less)
```

When asked how concerns about race or ethnicity differed between AI systems and simpler formula-based tools, opinions were divided: the largest group (`r fmt_ci_inner(pct_ai_none, ci_ai_none)`) expressed no concern about any tool and a similar proportion (`r fmt_ci_inner(pct_ai_equal, ci_ai_equal)`) were equally concerned regardless of type. Among those who differentiated, nearly three times as many were more concerned about AI (`r fmt_ci_inner(pct_ai_more, ci_ai_more)`) than less concerned (`r fmt_ci_inner(pct_ai_less, ci_ai_less)`).

```{r}
#| label: calc-stakeholder-input
#| output: false

# fd-stakeholder is a comma-separated multi-select field
stakeholder_n <- sum(!is.na(responses[["fd-stakeholder"]]))

pct_stakeholder <- function(label) {
  sum(str_detect(responses[["fd-stakeholder"]], fixed(label)), na.rm = TRUE) /
    stakeholder_n * 100
}

boot_ci_stakeholder <- function(label, R = 2000) {
  vec <- responses[["fd-stakeholder"]]
  vec <- vec[!is.na(vec)]
  hits <- str_detect(vec, fixed(label))
  reps <- replicate(R, mean(sample(hits, length(hits), replace = TRUE)) * 100)
  quantile(reps, c(0.025, 0.975), names = FALSE)
}

pct_sk_research  <- pct_stakeholder("Medical researchers and scientists")
ci_sk_research   <- boot_ci_stakeholder("Medical researchers and scientists")
pct_sk_provider  <- pct_stakeholder("Doctors and healthcare providers")
ci_sk_provider   <- boot_ci_stakeholder("Doctors and healthcare providers")
pct_sk_patient   <- pct_stakeholder("Individual patients (for decisions about their own care)")
ci_sk_patient    <- boot_ci_stakeholder("Individual patients (for decisions about their own care)")
pct_sk_govt      <- pct_stakeholder("Government or public health agencies")
ci_sk_govt       <- boot_ci_stakeholder("Government or public health agencies")
pct_sk_advocacy  <- pct_stakeholder("Patient advocacy groups or organizations")
ci_sk_advocacy   <- boot_ci_stakeholder("Patient advocacy groups or organizations")
pct_sk_public    <- pct_stakeholder("The general public")
ci_sk_public     <- boot_ci_stakeholder("The general public")
```

When asked who should have input on race or ethnicity in clinical calculators, `r fmt_ci(pct_sk_research, ci_sk_research)` said medical researchers, `r fmt_ci(pct_sk_provider, ci_sk_provider)` healthcare providers, `r fmt_ci(pct_sk_patient, ci_sk_patient)` individual patients for their own care, `r fmt_ci(pct_sk_govt, ci_sk_govt)` government or public health agencies, `r fmt_ci(pct_sk_advocacy, ci_sk_advocacy)` patient advocacy groups, and `r fmt_ci(pct_sk_public, ci_sk_public)` general public.

```{r}
#| label: fig-reaction
#| fig-width: 10
#| fig-height: 8
#| fig-cap: "Respondent reactions to race-specific algorithms and preferences for their revised counterparts. The upper three panels show agreement with three statements per algorithm (5-point Likert scale): *Represented* ('I feel represented by the race or ethnicity categories used to [interpret lung function test results / estimate kidney function / estimate heart disease risk / estimate bone fracture risk]'); *Worry harm* ('I worry that using my race or ethnicity in [spirometry / kidney function tests / heart disease risk calculators / the FRAX calculator] to support clinical decisions might harm me'); and *Helps care* ('I believe that using race or ethnicity in [spirometry / kidney function estimation / heart disease risk calculator / the FRAX calculator] could help ensure better care for me'). The lower panel shows preference for the revised race-free version over the race-specific original, among the three algorithms with a revised counterpart; FRAX has no revised version. 'Prefer to self-describe' responses are included in Neutral/Unsure. For all panels, bars extend rightward for agreement or preference for the revised version (blue) and leftward for disagreement or preference for the race-based version (red), with neutral responses (yellow) centred at zero. Net agreement, or net preference for the revised version, is shown to the right of each bar."

algo_levels    <- c("GLI-2012", "2009 CKD-EPI", "2013 ASCVD", "FRAX")
all_dim_levels <- c("Represented", "Worry harm", "Helps care",
                    "Preference for revised version")

# ---- Likert data ----
likert_vars <- c(
  "spiro-questions_1", "spiro-questions_2", "spiro-questions_3",
  "egfr-questions_1", "egfr-questions_2", "egfr-questions_3",
  "cvd-questions_1", "cvd-questions_2", "cvd-questions_3",
  "frax-questions_1", "frax-questions_2", "frax-questions_3"
)

likert_df <- responses |>
  select(all_of(likert_vars)) |>
  setNames(c(
    "GLI-2012: Represented", "GLI-2012: Worry harm", "GLI-2012: Helps care",
    "2009 CKD-EPI: Represented", "2009 CKD-EPI: Worry harm", "2009 CKD-EPI: Helps care",
    "2013 ASCVD: Represented", "2013 ASCVD: Worry harm", "2013 ASCVD: Helps care",
    "FRAX: Represented", "FRAX: Worry harm", "FRAX: Helps care"
  )) |>
  pivot_longer(everything(), names_to = "question", values_to = "response") |>
  filter(!is.na(response)) |>
  mutate(
    algorithm = str_extract(question, "^[^:]+"),
    dimension = str_extract(question, "(?<=: ).+"),
    response  = factor(response, levels = likert_levels)
  )

likert_full <- likert_df |>
  count(algorithm, dimension, response) |>
  group_by(algorithm, dimension) |>
  mutate(pct = n / sum(n) * 100) |>
  ungroup() |>
  mutate(
    response_num = as.numeric(response),
    dimension    = factor(dimension, levels = c("Represented", "Worry harm", "Helps care"))
  )

likert_diverging <- likert_full |>
  group_by(algorithm, dimension) |>
  mutate(
    neutral_pct = pct[response_num == 3],
    xmin = case_when(
      response_num == 1 ~ -(pct[response_num == 2] + pct[response_num == 1] + neutral_pct / 2),
      response_num == 2 ~ -(pct[response_num == 2] + neutral_pct / 2),
      response_num == 3 ~ -neutral_pct / 2,
      response_num == 4 ~ neutral_pct / 2,
      response_num == 5 ~ pct[response_num == 4] + neutral_pct / 2
    ),
    xmax = case_when(
      response_num == 1 ~ -(pct[response_num == 2] + neutral_pct / 2),
      response_num == 2 ~ -neutral_pct / 2,
      response_num == 3 ~ neutral_pct / 2,
      response_num == 4 ~ pct[response_num == 4] + neutral_pct / 2,
      response_num == 5 ~ pct[response_num == 4] + pct[response_num == 5] + neutral_pct / 2
    )
  ) |>
  ungroup() |>
  mutate(
    algorithm = factor(algorithm, levels = algo_levels),
    dimension = factor(as.character(dimension), levels = all_dim_levels),
    response  = as.character(response)
  )

# ---- Preference data (4th panel) ----
pref_algo_map <- c(
  "spiro-new-reaction" = "GLI-2012",
  "egfr-new-reaction"  = "2009 CKD-EPI",
  "cvd-new-reaction"   = "2013 ASCVD"
)

pref_collapse <- c(
  "Prefer race-based"                 = "Prefer race-based",
  "Neutral/Unsure"                    = "Neutral/Unsure",
  "Other"                             = "Neutral/Unsure",
  "Prefer race-free"                  = "Prefer revised version",
  "Prefer postal-ZIP instead of race" = "Prefer revised version"
)

pref_num <- c(
  "Prefer race-based"      = 1L,
  "Neutral/Unsure"         = 3L,
  "Prefer revised version" = 5L
)

pref_full <- imap_dfr(pref_algo_map, function(algo, var) {
  v    <- simplify_reaction(responses[[var]])
  v    <- v[!is.na(v)]
  resp <- pref_collapse[v]
  tibble(algorithm = algo, response = resp[!is.na(resp)])
}) |>
  count(algorithm, response) |>
  group_by(algorithm) |>
  mutate(pct = n / sum(n) * 100) |>
  ungroup() |>
  mutate(
    response_num = pref_num[response],
    algorithm    = factor(algorithm, levels = algo_levels),
    dimension    = factor("Preference for revised version", levels = all_dim_levels)
  )

pref_diverging <- pref_full |>
  group_by(algorithm) |>
  mutate(
    neutral_pct = sum(pct[response_num == 3]),
    xmin = case_when(
      response_num == 1 ~ -(sum(pct[response_num == 1]) + neutral_pct / 2),
      response_num == 3 ~ -neutral_pct / 2,
      response_num == 4 ~ neutral_pct / 2,
      response_num == 5 ~ sum(pct[response_num == 4]) + neutral_pct / 2
    ),
    xmax = case_when(
      response_num == 1 ~ -neutral_pct / 2,
      response_num == 3 ~ neutral_pct / 2,
      response_num == 4 ~ sum(pct[response_num == 4]) + neutral_pct / 2,
      response_num == 5 ~ sum(pct[response_num == 4]) + sum(pct[response_num == 5]) + neutral_pct / 2
    )
  ) |>
  ungroup()

# ---- Combine ----
combined_diverging <- bind_rows(
  likert_diverging |> select(algorithm, dimension, response, response_num, pct, xmin, xmax),
  pref_diverging   |> select(algorithm, dimension, response, response_num, pct, xmin, xmax)
) |>
  mutate(
    algorithm = factor(algorithm, levels = algo_levels),
    dimension = factor(dimension, levels = all_dim_levels)
  )

net_labels_combined <- combined_diverging |>
  group_by(algorithm, dimension) |>
  summarise(
    net   = sum(pct[response_num %in% c(4, 5)]) - sum(pct[response_num %in% c(1, 2)]),
    x_end = max(xmax),
    .groups = "drop"
  )

combined_hex <- c(
  "Strongly disagree"          = "#d73027",
  "Somewhat disagree"          = "#fc8d59",
  "Neither agree nor disagree" = "#fee090",
  "Somewhat agree"             = "#91bfdb",
  "Strongly agree"             = "#4575b4",
  "Prefer race-based"          = "#d73027",
  "Neutral/Unsure"             = "#fee090",
  "Prefer revised version"     = "#4575b4"
)

legend_breaks <- c(
  "Strongly disagree", "Somewhat disagree", "Neither agree nor disagree",
  "Somewhat agree", "Strongly agree"
)

pref_key <- tibble(
  algorithm = factor("FRAX", levels = algo_levels),
  dimension = factor("Preference for revised version", levels = all_dim_levels),
  x         = c(-25, 0, 25),
  label     = c("Prefer race-based", "Neutral / Unsure", "Prefer revised version"),
  hex       = c("#d73027", "#8c7d2b", "#4575b4")
)

dimension_labels <- c(
  "Represented"                  = "Felt represented by the race or ethnicity categories",
  "Worry harm"                   = "Worried using race or ethnicity might harm them",
  "Helps care"                   = "Believed using race or ethnicity helps ensure better care",
  "Preference for revised version" = "Preferred the revised race-free version (FRAX: no revised version)"
)

ggplot(combined_diverging, aes(y = algorithm, xmin = xmin, xmax = xmax, fill = response)) +
  geom_rect(aes(ymin = as.numeric(algorithm) - 0.4,
                ymax = as.numeric(algorithm) + 0.4)) +
  geom_text(aes(x = (xmin + xmax) / 2, y = algorithm,
                label = ifelse(abs(xmax - xmin) > 6, sprintf("%.1f%%", pct), "")),
            size = 3) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = 0, linewidth = 0.3, alpha = 0.3) +
  geom_text(data = net_labels_combined,
            aes(x = x_end + 1, y = algorithm, label = sprintf("%+.1f%%", net)),
            inherit.aes = FALSE, size = 3.5, hjust = 0) +
  geom_text(data = pref_key,
            aes(x = x, y = algorithm, label = label, color = hex),
            inherit.aes = FALSE, size = 3, fontface = "italic") +
  facet_wrap(~ dimension, ncol = 1, labeller = labeller(dimension = dimension_labels)) +
  scale_fill_manual(
    values = combined_hex,
    breaks = legend_breaks,
    guide  = guide_legend(nrow = 1)
  ) +
  scale_color_identity() +
  scale_x_continuous(labels = \(x) paste0(abs(x), "%"),
                     expand = expansion(mult = c(0.05, 0.15))) +
  labs(x = "Percent", y = NULL, fill = NULL) +
  theme_minimal() +
  theme(legend.position = "top",
        panel.grid.major.y = element_blank(),
        strip.text = element_text(size = 11))
```

Among 215 substantive open-ended responses to other concerns, recurring themes were oversimplification of broad categories like "Black", "White", or "Hispanic" (7.0%) and risk of bias or discrimination grounded in historical misuse (11.2%). Many participants would accept race-specific tools conditionally if shown to improve accuracy or outcomes (8.8%) or on a case-by-case basis by disease indication (7.9%). Notably, 17.2% supported using race in clinical contexts, reasoning that it carries biological implications or serves as a proxy for environmental or lifestyle factors. A smaller subset (2.8%) expressed full trust in providers and researchers. The codebook (@supptab-codebook-reform), code frequencies (@supptab-codebook-freq), and example responses are in the appendix.

### Self-Identification Shifts with Algorithm Categories

```{r}
#| warning: false
#| label: fig-ethnicity-sankey
#| fig-width: 12
#| fig-height: 8
#| fig-cap: "Alluvial (Sankey) diagram showing how racial and ethnic self-identification shifts as the available categories change across alternative classification systems used in clinical calculators. Each vertical bar (stratum) represents one system: survey ethnicity, the single free-choice category participants selected when they signed up for the survey platform, followed by the race/ethnicity categories offered by spirometry references (GLI), eGFR, and cardiovascular risk (pooled cohort) algorithms. Each flowing ribbon represents respondents who shared the same combination of choices across all four systems; ribbon width is proportional to the number of respondents on that path. Ribbons that fan out or merge across columns indicate that respondents using one label did not consistently use the same label in the next system. The extensive criss-crossing visible throughout the diagram illustrates that self-identification is context-dependent: the categories offered shape the choices people make. This is especially evident for groups absent from certain algorithm category sets. For example, GLI-2012 spirometry references offer no dedicated Middle Eastern or Hispanic/Latino option, yet only 40.6% of Middle Eastern and 37.5% of Hispanic/Latino respondents chose 'White', the category algorithm developers had intended for them. Respondents who declined to answer are shown separately (Declined)."

algo_data <- responses |>
  filter(!is.na(Ethnicity),
         !is.na(`spiro-race-response`),
         !is.na(`egfr-race-response`),
         !is.na(`cvd-race-response`)) |>
  transmute(
    prolific_ethnicity = Ethnicity,
    spiro_race = if_else(tolower(`spiro-race-response`) == "prefer not to answer", "Declined", `spiro-race-response`),
    egfr_race  = if_else(tolower(`egfr-race-response`)  == "prefer not to answer", "Declined", `egfr-race-response`),
    cvd_race   = if_else(tolower(`cvd-race-response`)   == "prefer not to answer", "Declined", `cvd-race-response`)
  ) |>
  count(prolific_ethnicity, spiro_race, egfr_race, cvd_race, name = "n") |>
  mutate(
    prolific_ethnicity = factor(prolific_ethnicity, levels = sort(unique(prolific_ethnicity))),
    spiro_race = factor(spiro_race,
                        levels = c(sort(setdiff(unique(spiro_race), "Declined")), "Declined")),
    egfr_race  = factor(egfr_race,
                        levels = c(sort(setdiff(unique(egfr_race), "Declined")), "Declined")),
    cvd_race   = factor(cvd_race,
                        levels = c(sort(setdiff(unique(cvd_race), "Declined")), "Declined"))
  )

ggplot(algo_data,
       aes(axis1 = prolific_ethnicity, axis2 = spiro_race,
           axis3 = egfr_race, axis4 = cvd_race,
           y = n)) +
  geom_alluvium(aes(fill = prolific_ethnicity), width = 1/4, alpha = 0.7, discern = TRUE) +
  geom_stratum(width = 1/4, fill = "white", color = "grey70", linewidth = 0.1, discern = TRUE) +
  geom_text(stat = "stratum", discern = TRUE,
            aes(label = after_stat(stringr::str_wrap(sub("\\.[0-9]+$", "", as.character(stratum)), width = 12))),
            size = 2.5) +
  scale_x_discrete(limits = c( "Survey Ethnicity\n(single choice)",
                               "Spirometry\n(GLI)",
                               "eGFR",
                               "CVD (Pooled Cohort)"),
                   expand = c(0.15, 0.05)) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = prolific_eth_colors, guide = "none") +
  labs(y = "Number of respondents") +
  theme_minimal() +
  theme(
    axis.text.y = element_blank(),
    axis.ticks = element_blank(),
    panel.grid = element_blank()
  )
```

```{r}
#| label: sankey-stats
#| output: false

responses |>
  filter(Ethnicity %in% c("African", "Black/African American", "South Asian", "East Asian")) |>
  select(Ethnicity, `spiro-race-response`, `egfr-race-response`, `cvd-race-response`) |>
  pivot_longer(cols = -Ethnicity, names_to = "algorithm", values_to = "response") |>
  count(Ethnicity, algorithm, response) |>
  group_by(Ethnicity, algorithm) |>
  mutate(pct = round(n / sum(n) * 100)) |>
  ungroup() |>
  arrange(Ethnicity, algorithm, desc(n))
```

```{r}
#| label: calc-gli-white-stats
#| output: false

gli_white_pct_ci <- function(eth) {
  v <- responses[["spiro-race-response"]][responses$Ethnicity == eth]
  v <- v[!is.na(v)]
  hits <- v == "White"
  reps <- replicate(2000, mean(sample(hits, length(hits), replace = TRUE)) * 100)
  list(pct = mean(hits) * 100, ci = quantile(reps, c(0.025, 0.975), names = FALSE))
}

gli_me  <- gli_white_pct_ci("Middle Eastern")
gli_lat <- gli_white_pct_ci("Latino/Hispanic")
```

Participants' self-identification shifted with the categories offered by different clinical algorithms (@fig-ethnicity-sankey). Multiethnic individuals (@suppfig-ethnicity-upset; @suppfig-ethnicity-concordance) and populations often excluded from algorithm categories were more likely to self-classify inconsistently with developers' intent. For example, although GLI-2012 developers considered Middle Eastern and Hispanic individuals as part of the White category [@quanjer_multi-ethnic_2012], only `r fmt_ci(gli_me$pct, gli_me$ci)` of Middle Eastern and `r fmt_ci(gli_lat$pct, gli_lat$ci)` of Latino/Hispanic respondents self-classified as White when offered GLI-2012 categories.

### Experience of Racism

```{r}
#| label: race_misclassify
#| output: false

# question: Have you ever had the experience of noticing that a doctor, nurse, or clinic staff have filled out your race or ethnicity on a form or computer screen without asking you?
responses |>
   filter(!is.na(`rep-misclassify`)) |>
   count(`rep-misclassify`) |>
   mutate(pct = n / sum(n) * 100)

```

```{r}
#| label: calc-racism-bias-stats
#| output: false

racism_x <- responses[["racism-experience"]]
pct_racism_overall <- pct_match(racism_x, "Yes")
ci_racism_overall  <- boot_ci_match(racism_x, "Yes")

racism_by_eth <- responses |>
  filter(!is.na(`demo-ethnicity`)) |>
  rowwise() |>
  mutate(eth_list = list(names(ethnicity_categories_early)[
    sapply(ethnicity_categories_early, \(pat) str_detect(`demo-ethnicity`, pat))
  ])) |>
  ungroup() |>
  unnest(eth_list)

racism_pct_ci <- function(eth) {
  v <- racism_by_eth[["racism-experience"]][racism_by_eth$eth_list == eth]
  list(pct = pct_match(v, "Yes"), ci = boot_ci_match(v, "Yes"))
}
racism_white     <- racism_pct_ci("White")
racism_caribbean <- racism_pct_ci("Caribbean")

# rep-bias-problem: denominator excludes "Unsure"
bias_x <- responses[["rep-bias-problem"]]
bias_x <- bias_x[!is.na(bias_x) & bias_x != "Unsure"]
pct_bias_major <- pct_match(bias_x, "A major problem")
ci_bias_major  <- boot_ci_match(bias_x, "A major problem")
pct_bias_minor <- pct_match(bias_x, "A minor problem")
ci_bias_minor  <- boot_ci_match(bias_x, "A minor problem")
pct_bias_none  <- pct_match(bias_x, "Not a problem")
ci_bias_none   <- boot_ci_match(bias_x, "Not a problem")
```

Overall, `r fmt_ci(pct_racism_overall, ci_racism_overall)` of participants reported unfair healthcare treatment because of their race or ethnicity, ranging from `r fmt_ci(racism_white$pct, racism_white$ci)` among White participants to `r fmt_ci(racism_caribbean$pct, racism_caribbean$ci)` among Caribbeans. About `r fmt_ci(pct_bias_major, ci_bias_major)` viewed racial bias as a major problem in healthcare, `r fmt_ci(pct_bias_minor, ci_bias_minor)` as minor, and `r fmt_ci(pct_bias_none, ci_bias_none)` as not a problem (@suppfig-rep-bias).

We repeated the analysis among those who had experienced racism in healthcare (@supptab-characteristics). They expressed lower net comfort with every predictor (@suppfig-racism-comfort-factor), with the largest drops for race/ethnicity (+62.4% vs. +41.6%) and ZIP or postal code (+14.5% vs. +7.1%), and were less likely to feel represented by existing categories (@suppfig-racism-reaction-race-specific; e.g., GLI-2012 +25.7% vs. +12.2%, FRAX +42.8% vs. +26.4%). Most notably, while the full sample disagreed that race-specific algorithms could cause harm (net -21.2% to -28.5%), this subgroup shifted toward agreement (net -3.0% to +6.6%). Despite these concerns, a majority still agreed that using race helps improve care, though net agreement was lower (e.g., +24.9% vs. +38.9% for GLI-2012).

```{r}
#| label: calc-racism-spiro-stats
#| output: false

racism_spiro_react <- simplify_reaction(
  responses[["spiro-new-reaction"]][responses[["racism-experience"]] == "Yes"]
)
pct_racism_spiro_rf <- pct_match(racism_spiro_react, "Prefer race-free")
ci_racism_spiro_rf  <- boot_ci_match(racism_spiro_react, "Prefer race-free")
pct_racism_spiro_rb <- pct_match(racism_spiro_react, "Prefer race-based")
ci_racism_spiro_rb  <- boot_ci_match(racism_spiro_react, "Prefer race-based")
```

When asked about revised race-free algorithms (@suppfig-racism-perceptions-revised-algorithms), those who had experienced racism showed greater preference for the revised versions, though most still preferred the race-specific version, except for spirometry, where `r fmt_ci(pct_racism_spiro_rf, ci_racism_spiro_rf)` preferred race-averaged GLI-Global over `r fmt_ci(pct_racism_spiro_rb, ci_racism_spiro_rb)` who preferred race-specific GLI-2012.

About 9.4% of participants shared experiences of racism in healthcare; of 95 responses, 2 were excluded for non-substantive content and 3 for being outside healthcare. The most common instances involved differential treatment such as poorer provider attitudes or quality of care (30.0%), dismissive or neglectful behaviour (28.9%), and longer wait times or lower priority (22.2%). Participants also reported stereotypical assumptions about pain tolerance, background, lifestyle, or socioeconomic status, and attitudes towards individuals with mixed backgrounds, particularly among Indigenous respondents. The codebook (@supptab-codebook-racism), code frequencies (@supptab-codebook-freq), and example responses are in the appendix.

## Discussion

Our multinational survey, while not representative, captured opinions across diverse cultures and geographies, with several key findings. First, most respondents were comfortable with race or ethnicity as a predictor in clinical calculators (`r paste0(round(pct_race_comfort, 1),"%")`); this held across countries, self-identified groups, and among those who had experienced racism in healthcare. Second, across spirometry, eGFR, and cardiovascular risk calculators, 40.0% to 47.6% preferred race-specific versions, whereas 16.7% to 28.2% preferred race-free alternatives. Third, a substantial proportion did not find themselves represented in race and ethnicity categories, from 22.1% for FRAX to 43.9% for pooled cohort equations. Fourth, 2.5 times as many respondents were uncomfortable with postal or ZIP code as with race or ethnicity, even though postal or ZIP code has been adopted in some revised algorithms.

Although many respondents described race or ethnicity in biological terms, its fluidity was evident in our participants' shifting self-identification with different categories. Race and ethnicity are socially determined constructs [@bonilla-silva1999] with complex biological associations [@rose2023; @holland2008]. Our findings are consistent with literature showing that recorded race or ethnicity varies with who observes it [@roth2022; @herman2010], when [@liebler2017], social status cues [@freeman2011; @saperstein2014], and the classification scheme [@nicolas2018; @harris2002], sometimes with significant consequences [@movva_coarse; @Adibi2025a].

Prior US-focused work has reached similar conclusions. Diao et al. [@diao2026] surveyed 1,750 US adults and found 79.8% preferred their physician use all available information including race, and only 22.0% agreed there are "no circumstances under which a doctor should use my race in clinical care." More respondents were uncomfortable with income (39.3%) or ZIP code (22.3%) than race (8.8%). Our multinational sample was younger, more racially and ethnically diverse, and more likely to view racism as a major problem in healthcare, yet was still less likely to believe doctors should never use race or ethnicity (12.8%), and more uncomfortable with postal or ZIP code (32.6%).

These surveys show that seeking community input can yield actionable insights. The widespread discomfort with ZIP or postal code suggests that replacing race or ethnicity with an area-based deprivation score may not be perceived as more trustworthy by patients [@Adibi2025]. At least three widely used cardiovascular risk calculators—the UK's QRISK3 [@hippisley-cox2017], the American Heart Association's PREVENT [@khan2024], and Scotland's ASSIGN [@woodward2006]—use postal or ZIP code as an optional input to look up area-based deprivation indices. Future studies should examine how often patients volunteer their postal or ZIP codes when doctors use these tools, or how often these data are used without disclosure.

Our findings suggest a disconnect between public perspectives and the emerging trend in clinical practice to remove race and ethnicity from algorithms. In a US survey of 66 pulmonologists, 64% recommended revised race-averaged spirometry references versus 9% who recommended the race-specific version [@brems2026]. In a qualitative study of 23 patients at a Boston safety-net hospital, most were unaware that race was used in clinical calculators and felt it should not be, with Black participants reporting widespread mistrust driven by experiences of racism and fear of experimentation [@schmidt2023]. A separate study of 42 American stakeholders from universities, government, professional societies, and industry noted that clinicians and patients are often unaware of how widely algorithms are deployed and that algorithms can be biased regardless of whether they include race [@jain2023; @obermeyer2019; @pierson2021; @obermeyer2021; @zink2024; @siddique_impact_2024; @tipton2023; @cmss2023].

Several limitations apply. Our results reflect initial reactions: respondents were not primed with any arguments or evidence and might shift their views with such information. Our multinational design was not intended to yield representative samples of individual countries, and the Prolific participant pool skews younger and more educated and excludes populous nations such as China and Pakistan. Self-selection into studies by topic, reward rate, and survey length may also introduce hard-to-quantify response biases [@aksoy2025].

Decisions about what factors to include or exclude in clinical algorithms are not purely technical and involve many value judgments. Many philosophers of science have argued that researchers cannot avoid such judgments under uncertainty [@rudner1953; @douglas2000], and that ethical values informing them should reflect public values rather than expert values alone [@douglas2005; @douglas2009; @kitcher_science_2011]. These arguments are especially relevant to algorithmic reform given the historical and current realities of racism and discrimination in healthcare [@rethinki2025].

Recent medical society revisions to formerly race-specific algorithms in cardiology, nephrology, and pulmonology have wide-ranging implications for tens of millions of people in the US [@diao2024; @diao2024a; @Delgado2022] and potentially many more globally. Yet only the kidney function task force reported systematically seeking input from community members, patients, and caregivers [@Delgado2022]. The lack of widespread community consultation in algorithmic reform is a missed opportunity to raise awareness, align values, and preserve public trust.

US public confidence in medical societies such as the American Heart Association (82%) and American Medical Association (77%) remains high [@adams2026], even as trust in health institutions might be declining [@isthere2025; @kffpoll2026]. A recent survey of over 70,000 adults across 68 countries found that the public views scientists as having greater integrity than openness and concluded that scientists should pursue genuine dialogue rather than top-down communication [@cologna2025].

Professional medical societies and algorithm developers should engage with patient and public opinion regardless of whether their final recommendation is to remove or keep race and ethnicity as predictors.

    modify_footnote_body(

      rows = variable == "Employment status" & label == "Not in paid work"

Intersection analysis of self-reported ethnic identities among survey respondents. Horizontal bars (left) show the total number of respondents selecting each ethnicity. Vertical bars (top) show the frequency of each unique combination of ethnicities, ordered by size. Connected dots indicate multi-ethnic identifications. Approximately 30% of respondents selected two or more ethnic categories, reflecting the multi-dimensional nature of ethnic identity.
:::

::: {#suppfig-ethnicity-concordance}
```{r}
#| warning: false
#| fig-width: 8
#| fig-height: 7

# Denominator: unique respondents per Prolific category (original names)
prolific_totals <- responses |>
  filter(!is.na(`demo-ethnicity`), !is.na(Ethnicity)) |>
  count(prolific_ethnicity = Ethnicity, name = "total")

# Concordance matrix: for each Prolific category, % who selected each survey category
heatmap_data <- responses |>
  filter(!is.na(`demo-ethnicity`), !is.na(Ethnicity)) |>
  transmute(
    prolific_ethnicity = Ethnicity,
    African = str_detect(`demo-ethnicity`, "African \\("),
    `African American` = str_detect(`demo-ethnicity`, "African American"),
    Caribbean = str_detect(`demo-ethnicity`, "Caribbean"),
    `East Asian` = str_detect(`demo-ethnicity`, "East Asian"),
    `Hispanic/Latino` = str_detect(`demo-ethnicity`, "Hispanic"),
    Indigenous = str_detect(`demo-ethnicity`, "Indigenous"),
    `Middle Eastern/N. African` = str_detect(`demo-ethnicity`, "Middle Eastern"),
    `South Asian` = str_detect(`demo-ethnicity`, "(?<!east )South Asian"),
    `Southeast Asian` = str_detect(`demo-ethnicity`, "Southeast Asian"),
    White = str_detect(`demo-ethnicity`, "White")
  ) |>
  pivot_longer(cols = -prolific_ethnicity, names_to = "survey_ethnicity", values_to = "selected") |>
  filter(selected) |>
  count(prolific_ethnicity, survey_ethnicity, name = "n") |>
  left_join(prolific_totals, by = "prolific_ethnicity") |>
  mutate(
    pct = n / total * 100,
    prolific_ethnicity = factor(prolific_ethnicity, levels = rev(prolific_cat_order)),
    survey_ethnicity   = factor(survey_ethnicity,   levels = cat_order)
  )

ggplot(heatmap_data, aes(x = survey_ethnicity, y = prolific_ethnicity, fill = pct)) +
  geom_tile(color = "white", linewidth = 0.8) +
  geom_text(aes(label = ifelse(pct >= 2, sprintf("%.0f%%", pct), "")), size = 3) +
  scale_fill_gradient(low = "white", high = "#2166ac",
                      name = "Row %",
                      limits = c(0, 100)) +
  scale_x_discrete(labels = function(x) stringr::str_wrap(x, width = 10)) +
  labs(x = "Survey ethnicity (multi-select)", y = "Prolific ethnicity (single-choice)") +
  theme_minimal() +
  theme(
    axis.text.x = element_text(angle = 45, hjust = 1),
    panel.grid = element_blank()
  )
```

Heatmap comparing participants' self-reported ethnicity at Prolific sign-up (single-choice, rows) with their self-reported ethnicity in our survey (multi-select, columns). The Prolific classification was used for quota sampling. Cell color and labels show the percentage of respondents in each Prolific sign-up category who selected a given survey ethnicity; row percentages can exceed 100% because survey responses were multi-select. Diagonal cells represent within-category concordance; off-diagonal cells reveal cross-category identification.
:::

## Results Among Those Who Experienced Racism {#sec-racism-subgroup .appendix}

::: {#supptab-characteristics}
```{r}
ethnicity_cats <- c(
  "African \\(" = "African",
  "African American" = "African American",
  "Caribbean" = "Caribbean",
  "East Asian" = "East Asian",
  "Hispanic" = "Hispanic/Latino",
  "Indigenous" = "Indigenous",
  "Middle Eastern" = "Middle Eastern/North African",
  "(?<!east )South Asian" = "South Asian",
  "Southeast Asian" = "Southeast Asian",
  "White" = "White"
)

char_df <- responses |>
  mutate(
    `Experienced racism in healthcare` = if_else(
      `racism-experience` == "Yes", "Yes", "No", missing = "No"
    )
  ) |>
  mutate(across(
    all_of(setNames(rep("demo-ethnicity", length(ethnicity_cats)), ethnicity_cats)),
    .fns = ~ NULL
  ))

# Build ethnicity binary columns
for (i in seq_along(ethnicity_cats)) {
  pat <- names(ethnicity_cats)[i]
  lab <- ethnicity_cats[i]
  char_df[[lab]] <- factor(
    if_else(str_detect(char_df$`demo-ethnicity`, pat), "Yes", "No", missing = "No"),
    levels = c("Yes", "No")
  )
}

char_df |>
  select(
    `Age group`, Sex, Gender, `Employment status`, `Socioeconomic status`,
    all_of(unname(ethnicity_cats)),
    `Experienced racism in healthcare`
  ) |>
  mutate(
    across(c(Gender, `Employment status`), \(x) str_remove(x, "\\s*\\(.*\\)")),
    Gender = factor(
      if_else(is.na(Gender) | Gender == "Rather not say",
              "Rather not say / Unknown", Gender),
      levels = c("Woman", "Man", "Non-binary", "Rather not say / Unknown")
    ),
    `Employment status` = factor(`Employment status`,
      levels = c("Full-Time", "Part-Time", "Not in paid work", "Unemployed",
                 "Due to start a new job within the next month", "Other")) |>
      forcats::fct_na_value_to_level("Unknown"),
    `Socioeconomic status` = as.numeric(`Socioeconomic status`)
  ) |>
  tbl_summary(
    by = `Experienced racism in healthcare`,
    missing = "no",
    digits = list(all_continuous() ~ 1, all_categorical() ~ c(0, 0)),
    label = c(
      list(`Socioeconomic status` ~ "Socioeconomic status"),
      setNames(as.list(unname(ethnicity_cats)), unname(ethnicity_cats))
    ),
    type = setNames(
      replicate(length(ethnicity_cats), "dichotomous", simplify = FALSE),
      unname(ethnicity_cats)
    ),
    value = setNames(
      replicate(length(ethnicity_cats), "Yes", simplify = FALSE),
      unname(ethnicity_cats)
    )
  ) |>
    modify_footnote_body(
      footnote = "Sex as recorded on legal/official documents",
      columns = "label",
      rows = variable == "Sex" & row_type == "label"
    ) |>
    modify_footnote_body(
      footnote = "Participants were asked the following question: Where would you put yourself on the socioeconomic ladder? Choose between 1 to 10.",
      columns = "label",
      rows = variable == "Socioeconomic status" & row_type == "label"
    ) |>
    as_flex_table()
```

Characteristics of survey participants who reported unfair treatment due to race/ethnicity. Self-reported ethnicity categories are not mutually exclusive, as respondents could select multiple identities.

:::

```{r}
#| label: unfair-treatment-subset

unfair_subset <- responses |>
  filter(`racism-experience` == "Yes")

```

::: {#suppfig-racism-comfort-factor}
```{r}
#| label: suppfig-racism-comfort-factor
#| fig-width: 9
#| fig-height: 5

factor_vars <- c("fd-factors_1", "fd-factors_2", "fd-factors_3",
                 "fd-factors_4", "fd-factors_5", "fd-factors_6", "fd-factors_7")
factor_labels <- c("Age", "Biological sex", "Race/ethnicity",
                   "ZIP or Postal Code", "Environmental exposures", "Genetic ancestry", "Country of origin")

comfort_df_unfair <- unfair_subset |>
  select(all_of(factor_vars)) |>
  setNames(factor_labels) |>
  pivot_longer(everything(), names_to = "factor", values_to = "comfort") |>
  filter(!is.na(comfort)) |>
  mutate(comfort = factor(comfort, levels = comfort_levels))

comfort_summary_unfair <- comfort_df_unfair |>
  count(factor, comfort) |>
  group_by(factor) |>
  mutate(pct = n / sum(n) * 100) |>
  ungroup()

factor_order_unfair <- comfort_summary_unfair |>
  mutate(side = case_when(
    comfort %in% c("Somewhat comfortable", "Extremely comfortable") ~ "pos",
    comfort %in% c("Somewhat uncomfortable", "Extremely uncomfortable") ~ "neg",
    TRUE ~ "neutral"
  )) |>
  group_by(factor) |>
  summarise(
    net = sum(pct[side == "pos"]) - sum(pct[side == "neg"]),
    .groups = "drop"
  ) |>
  arrange(net) |>
  pull(factor)

comfort_plot_unfair <- comfort_summary_unfair |>
  mutate(factor = factor(factor, levels = factor_order_unfair)) |>
  group_by(factor) |>
  mutate(
    neutral_pct = pct[comfort == "Neither comfortable nor uncomfortable"],
    xmin = case_when(
      comfort == "Extremely uncomfortable" ~
        -(pct[comfort == "Extremely uncomfortable"] +
          pct[comfort == "Somewhat uncomfortable"] +
          neutral_pct / 2),
      comfort == "Somewhat uncomfortable" ~
        -(pct[comfort == "Somewhat uncomfortable"] +
          neutral_pct / 2),
      comfort == "Neither comfortable nor uncomfortable" ~
        -(neutral_pct / 2),
      comfort == "Somewhat comfortable" ~
        neutral_pct / 2,
      comfort == "Extremely comfortable" ~
        neutral_pct / 2 + pct[comfort == "Somewhat comfortable"]
    ),
    xmax = xmin + pct
  ) |>
  ungroup()

net_labels_unfair <- comfort_plot_unfair |>
  group_by(factor) |>
  summarise(
    net = sum(pct[comfort %in% c("Somewhat comfortable", "Extremely comfortable")]) -
          sum(pct[comfort %in% c("Somewhat uncomfortable", "Extremely uncomfortable")]),
    x_end = max(xmax),
    .groups = "drop"
  )

ggplot(comfort_plot_unfair, aes(y = factor, xmin = xmin, xmax = xmax, fill = comfort)) +
  geom_rect(aes(ymin = as.numeric(factor) - 0.35,
                ymax = as.numeric(factor) + 0.35)) +
  geom_text(aes(x = (xmin + xmax) / 2, y = factor,
                label = ifelse(abs(xmax - xmin) > 6, sprintf("%.1f%%", pct), "")),
            size = 3) +
  geom_text(data = net_labels_unfair,
            aes(x = x_end + 2, y = factor, label = sprintf("%+.1f%%", net)),
            inherit.aes = FALSE, size = 3.5, hjust = 0) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = 0, linewidth = 0.3, alpha = 0.3) +
  scale_fill_manual(
    values = c(
      "Extremely uncomfortable" = "#d73027",
      "Somewhat uncomfortable"  = "#fc8d59",
      "Neither comfortable nor uncomfortable" = "#cccccc",
      "Somewhat comfortable"    = "#91bfdb",
      "Extremely comfortable"   = "#4575b4"
    ),
    name = NULL,
    breaks = comfort_levels
  ) +
  scale_x_continuous(labels = \(x) paste0(abs(x), "%"),
                     expand = expansion(mult = c(0.05, 0.12))) +
  labs(x = NULL, y = NULL) +
  theme_minimal() +
  guides(fill = guide_legend(nrow = 2, byrow = TRUE)) +
  theme(legend.position = "top",
        legend.text = element_text(size = 8))
```

Comfort with calculator factors among respondents who reported unfair treatment due to race/ethnicity.
:::

```{r}
#| output: false
#| 
likert_df_unfair <- unfair_subset |>
  select(all_of(likert_vars)) |>
  setNames(c(
    "GLI-2012: Represented", "GLI-2012: Worry harm", "GLI-2012: Helps care",
    "2009 CKD-EPI: Represented", "2009 CKD-EPI: Worry harm", "2009 CKD-EPI: Helps care",

  )) |>

    response = factor(response, levels = likert_levels)
  )
```

::: {#suppfig-racism-reaction-race-specific}
```{r}
#| label: suppfig-racism-reaction-race-specific
#| fig-width: 10
#| fig-height: 7

likert_full_unfair <- likert_df_unfair |>
  count(algorithm, dimension, response) |>
  group_by(algorithm, dimension) |>
  mutate(pct = n / sum(n) * 100) |>
  ungroup() |>
  mutate(
    response_num = as.numeric(response),
    dimension = factor(dimension, levels = c("Represented", "Worry harm", "Helps care")),
    question_label = paste(algorithm, dimension, sep = ": ")
  )

likert_diverging_unfair <- likert_full_unfair |>
  group_by(algorithm, dimension) |>
  mutate(
    neutral_pct = pct[response_num == 3],
    xmin = case_when(
      response_num == 1 ~ -(pct[response_num == 2] + pct[response_num == 1] + neutral_pct / 2),
      response_num == 2 ~ -(pct[response_num == 2] + neutral_pct / 2),
      response_num == 3 ~ -neutral_pct / 2,
      response_num == 4 ~ neutral_pct / 2,
      response_num == 5 ~ pct[response_num == 4] + neutral_pct / 2
    ),
    xmax = case_when(
      response_num == 1 ~ -(pct[response_num == 2] + neutral_pct / 2),
      response_num == 2 ~ -neutral_pct / 2,
      response_num == 3 ~ neutral_pct / 2,
      response_num == 4 ~ pct[response_num == 4] + neutral_pct / 2,
      response_num == 5 ~ pct[response_num == 4] + pct[response_num == 5] + neutral_pct / 2
    )
  ) |>
  ungroup()

net_labels_likert_unfair <- likert_diverging_unfair |>
  group_by(algorithm, dimension) |>
  summarise(
    net = sum(pct[response_num %in% c(4, 5)]) - sum(pct[response_num %in% c(1, 2)]),
    x_end = max(xmax),
    .groups = "drop"
  )

ggplot(likert_diverging_unfair, aes(y = algorithm, xmin = xmin, xmax = xmax, fill = response)) +
  geom_rect(aes(ymin = as.numeric(factor(algorithm)) - 0.4,
                ymax = as.numeric(factor(algorithm)) + 0.4)) +
  geom_text(aes(x = (xmin + xmax) / 2, y = algorithm,
                label = ifelse(abs(xmax - xmin) > 6, sprintf("%.1f%%", pct), "")),
            size = 3) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = 0, linewidth = 0.3, alpha = 0.3) +
  geom_text(data = net_labels_likert_unfair,
            aes(x = x_end + 2, y = algorithm, label = sprintf("%+.1f%%", net)),
            inherit.aes = FALSE, size = 3.5, hjust = 0) +
  facet_wrap(~ dimension, ncol = 1, labeller = labeller(dimension = dimension_labels)) +
  scale_fill_manual(
    values = c(
      "Strongly disagree" = "#d73027",
      "Somewhat disagree" = "#fc8d59",
      "Neither agree nor disagree" = "#fee090",
      "Somewhat agree" = "#91bfdb",
      "Strongly agree" = "#4575b4"
    ),
    guide = guide_legend(nrow = 1)
  ) +
  scale_x_continuous(labels = \(x) paste0(abs(x), "%")) +
  labs(x = "Percent", y = NULL, fill = NULL) +
  theme_minimal() +
  theme(legend.position = "bottom",
        panel.grid.major.y = element_blank(),
        strip.text = element_text(size = 11))
```

Respondent reactions to race-specific algorithms among those who reported unfair treatment due to race/ethnicity. Bars extend rightward for agreement (light and dark blue) and leftward for disagreement (light and dark red), with neutral responses (yellow) centred at zero. Net agreement (total percentage agreeing minus total percentage disagreeing) is shown to the right of each bar.
